name: Coast folk
one_line: The sea was a garden already, so they never farmed: weirs, middens and salt, and towns without a single seed.

needs: a stream or spring for fresh water

staples: salmon or herring runs in season
how: line and hook from the rocks
preserve: drying on racks in the wind

fuel.note: driftwood from the tide line; dune grass for kindling; a maritime forest adds branch

shelter.form: low houses turned from the wind, a drying rack beside each, an upturned boat as a roof

ROCKY_SHORE.food: cod and shellfish dried on cold rock
ROCKY_SHORE.shelter: sod and whalebone in the lee of the rock

BEACH.food: clams from the garden, surf fish

DUNES.shelter: dug into the lee of a dune

ESTUARY.food: eels, mullet, the weir's best catch
ESTUARY.shelter: plank on stilts over the mud

SALT_MARSH.shelter: reed and driftwood on a hummock

knows: seaweed (kelp, dulse) as food and salt
plantkeeper.teaches_flavour: which seaweed to eat raw and which to dry; why the midden grows different plants
plantkeeper.teaches_practical: red tide months when shellfish kill; sea buckthorn against scurvy

techniques.name: Line and hook
techniques.verb: twist a line, carve a hook of bone or shell, cut a pole
techniques.teaches: the patient way to fish; the spear stays the fast way
techniques.unlocks: the player fishes with a pole and line

techniques.name: The weir
techniques.verb: drive stakes in a V at the tideline; the tide comes in over it and goes out, and the fish are left behind the fence
techniques.teaches: no skill, no luck, just geometry and patience: what let people build towns without a seed
techniques.unlocks: the camp's fish_run ceiling; the player can build one at a suitable shore

techniques.name: Clam garden
techniques.verb: wall a beach terrace at the low-tide line; clams thrive in the flat behind it
techniques.teaches: a shellfish crop with no seed, tended for centuries

techniques.name: Salt pans
techniques.verb: seawater in a shallow rock pan; the sun does the work
techniques.teaches: salt makes food keep; it is what the coast trades inland

techniques.name: Drying racks
techniques.verb: racks in the wind, or over a slow smoky fire
techniques.unlocks: fish keep through the lean season

techniques.name: Fat lamp
techniques.verb: a stone bowl, rendered seal or fish fat, a moss wick
techniques.teaches: light that burns for hours and does not blow out
techniques.unlocks: a lamp to set down inside a shelter

ladder: fire in the lee of the rock
drying racks and the midden begins
salt goes inland on the road
growth.restraint: a weir takes only what the tide gives; the clam garden is tended, never stripped; the midden grows a hill over centuries without the shore emptying
growth.ceiling_hint: the richest coast (a salmon run) reaches the tribal ceiling; a bare beach stays a handful

signatures.what: a mound of shell a different colour from the shore; lime-rich, so different plants grow on it
signatures.restore: cleared: the new camp's midden starts on the old one
signatures.inherits: nothing but the site's proof that it fed people

signatures.what: a V of stake stubs in the tideline, visible at low tide
signatures.restore: restored: new stakes on the old line
signatures.inherits: the weir works from the first season

signatures.what: shallow pans cut in shoreline rock
signatures.restore: restored: cleared of weed and sand

signatures.what: rectangular hollows in the turf where plank houses stood
signatures.restore: restored: the camp builds on the old floors

ruin.plants_differ: lime-loving plants on the midden (nettle, elder, mallow) in a shore that otherwise grows grass and thrift

aesthetic.silhouette: low, wind-turned houses; racks of fish like flags; an upturned boat

real_world.analogue: Pacific Northwest peoples (Coast Salish, Haida, Tlingit, Nuu-chah-nulth)
real_world.note: salmon runs, cedar plank houses, clam gardens terraced into the beach; large permanent towns with no farming
shell middens by the thousand, pottery ten thousand years old, settled foraging
kitchen middens (køkkenmøddinger) on the shore; fish weirs in the fjords
stake weirs at the tideline are among the oldest fixed structures; the Boylston Street weir in Boston is ~5,000 years old
